facts.fact: Books preserved sacred texts, science and heritage and passed knowledge across generations.
The Vedas, Upanishads and Puranas were considered divine revelations.
Books formed the core of Gurukul education.
Books were written in Sanskrit, Prakrit and regional languages.
The Bhagavad Gita and Manusmriti gave ethical and moral guidance.
The Arthashastra and the Mudrarakshasa are works of political literature (statecraft).
The Natyashastra, the treatise on drama, dance and music, is attributed to Bharata Muni.
The Rigveda was composed by many sages such as Gritsamada, Vishwamitra and Vamadeva.
The Rigveda has 1,028 hymns in 10 Mandalas.
The Rigveda is dated c. 1500–1200 BCE.
Rigvedic hymns are addressed to deities like Agni, Indra and Soma.
The Gayatri Mantra, in the Rigveda (Mandala III), is credited to Vishwamitra.
The Samaveda, derived from the Rigveda, gives melodies (Saman) for chanting.
The Yajurveda contains prose and verse for conducting sacrifices.
The Atharvaveda contains spells and incantations about medicine and daily life.
The Brahmanas are commentaries explaining Vedic rituals, composed by priests.
The Aranyakas are 'forest texts' for meditation, composed by hermits.
The Upanishads are philosophical treatises, the foundation of Vedanta.
Shatapatha Brahmana was written by Yajnavalkya — linked to the Yajurveda.
Aitareya Brahmana was written by Mahidasa Aitareya — linked to the Rigveda.
Taittiriya Brahmana was written by Tittiri (Yajurveda school).
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad was written by Yajnavalkya — on Atman and Brahman.
The Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Samaveda.
The Taittiriya Upanishad discusses education and self-discipline.
The Gopatha Brahmana belongs to the Atharvaveda.
'Satyameva Jayate' comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.
The Katha Upanishad tells the dialogue of Nachiketa and Yama.
Samkhya Sutras was written by Kapila — dualism of Purusha and Prakriti.
Manusmriti was written by Manu — a text on Dharma and law.
Yoga Sutra was written by Patanjali — founder text of the Yoga school.
Nyaya Sutra was written by Gautama (Akshapada) — logic.
Vaisheshika Sutra was written by Kanada — atomism.
Mimamsa Sutra was written by Jaimini — Vedic ritual interpretation.
Brahma Sutra was written by Badarayana — Vedanta.
Ashtadhyayi was written by Panini — Sanskrit grammar.
Vartika was written by Katyayana — notes on Panini.
Mahabhashya was written by Patanjali — great commentary on Panini.
Patanjali was a contemporary of the Shunga king Pushyamitra.
Katantra was written by Sarvavarman — a short Sanskrit grammar of the Satavahana court.
The Tripitaka (Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma Pitakas) was compiled by Buddhist councils in Pali.
The Vinaya Pitaka contains the rules of monastic life.
Milinda Panha was written by Nagasena — a dialogue with King Milinda (Menander I).
Buddhacharita was written by Ashvaghosha — a Sanskrit epic on the Buddha's life.
Ashvaghosha was a court figure of the Kushana king Kanishka.
Saundarananda was written by Ashvaghosha — conversion of the Buddha's half-brother Nanda.
Visuddhimagga was written by Buddhaghosa — a Theravada manual.
Mahavamsa was written by Mahanama Thera — chronicle of Buddhism in Sri Lanka.
The Dipavamsa is the older Pali chronicle of Sri Lanka.
The Divyavadana is a Sanskrit collection of legends of the Buddha and his disciples.
The Jataka tales tell the stories of the Buddha's previous lives.
Abhidharmakosa was written by Vasubandhu — Abhidharma philosophy.
The Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita Hridaya) is a Mahayana text on wisdom and emptiness (Shunyata).
The Lankavatara Sutra teaches consciousness-only (Vijnanavada).
The Dhammapada is a collection of the Buddha's sayings, in Pali.
Madhyamika Karika was written by Nagarjuna — founder of the Madhyamika (Shunyavada) school; linked with Nagarjunakonda in Andhra.
The Agamas, Mahavira's teachings compiled by the Ganadharas, are in Prakrit.
Kalpasutra was written by Bhadrabahu — life of Mahavira and the Tirthankaras.
Niryukti was written by Bhadrabahu — commentary on Jain scriptures.
Tattvartha Sutra was written by Umaswati — accepted by both Digambaras and Svetambaras.
Samayasara was written by Kundakunda — nature of the soul.
Panchastikaya was written by Kundakunda — the five substances (Dravyas).
Niyamasara was written by Kundakunda — discipline for liberation.
The Acharanga Sutra focuses on Jain conduct, especially ahimsa.
The Sthananga Sutra discusses Jain cosmology and the categories of living beings.
The Bhagavati Sutra is an encyclopedic Jain text on cosmology and the soul.
Ratnakaranda Shravakachara was written by Samantabhadra — a manual for householders.
Gommatsara was written by Nemichandra — karma theory.
Prashamarati was written by Umaswati — inner peace and detachment.
Arthashastra was written by Kautilya (Chanakya) — statecraft, 4th century BCE.
Kautilya was also known as Chanakya and Vishnugupta.
Indica was written by Megasthenes — a Greek account of Mauryan India and Pataliputra.
Ashoka's edicts are in Prakrit, written in the Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts.
Mudrarakshasa was written by Vishakhadatta — a drama on Chanakya's establishment of Chandragupta Maurya.
Devichandraguptam was written by Vishakhadatta — a drama on Chandragupta II.
The Vishnu Purana gives an account of Chandragupta Maurya and the Mauryan dynasty.
Nitisara was written by Kamandaka — a Gupta-age treatise on polity based on the Arthashastra.
Gathasaptasati was written by Hala — a Prakrit anthology of 700 verses by the Satavahana king.
Brihatkatha was written by Gunadhya — written in Paishachi Prakrit at the Satavahana court.
Tolkappiyam was written by Tolkappiyar — the oldest Tamil grammar.
The Tolkappiyam has three parts: Ezhuthathikaram, Sollathikaram and Porulathikaram.
The Ettuthogai (Eight Anthologies) include Aingurunooru, Purananuru, Ahananuru, Narrinai, Kurunthogai, Paripadal, Kalithogai and Pathirruppathu.
The Purananuru is a collection of 400 poems on war, kingship and heroism.
The Akananuru is a collection of 400 poems on love.
Akam poems deal with love (inner life) and Puram poems with war and public life.
The Pathupattu (Ten Idylls) includes Tirumurugarruppadai, Porunarruppadai and Malaipadukadam.
Manimekalai was written by Seethalai Sathanar — a Buddhist epic, sequel to the Silappadikaram.
Silappadikaram was written by Ilango Adigal — the story of Kannagi's devotion and justice.
The heroine of the Silappadikaram is Kannagi.
Civaka Cintamani was written by Tirutakkadevar — a Jain epic (10th century per source).
The five great Tamil epics are Silappadikaram, Manimekalai, Civaka Cintamani, Valayapathi and Kundalakesi.
The Kurunthogai contains short poems on love and nature.
Tirukkural was written by Thiruvalluvar — 1,330 couplets, called the 'Tamil Bible'.
The Tirukkural has 1,330 couplets on ethics, polity and love and is called the 'Tamil Bible'.
The Paripadal has poems on love and devotion referring to Vishnu and Murugan.
Maduraikkanchi was written by Mangudi Maruthanar — describes the city of Madurai.
The Kalithogai is a collection of 150 poems on love and nature.
The Pathirruppathu praises the Chera kings.
Malaipadukadam was written by Perunkunrur Perunkaucikanar — a journey to the hill country.
Ramayana was written by Valmiki — the Adi Kavi.
Mahabharata was written by Ved Vyasa — the Kurukshetra war.
The Bhagavad Gita is a philosophical discourse within the Mahabharata.
The Harivamsa, attributed to Vyasa, is an appendix to the Mahabharata on Krishna and the Yadavas.
Mrichchhakatika (The Little Clay Cart) was written by Shudraka.
Mrichchhakatika means 'The Little Clay Cart'.
Aryabhatiya was written by Aryabhata — astronomy and mathematics, 499 CE.
The Aryabhatiya was written in 499 CE.
Brahmasphutasiddhanta was written by Brahmagupta — 628 CE; rules for zero and negative numbers.
Brahmagupta first gave rules for zero and negative numbers; the source also credits Aryabhata with zero.
Kamasutra was written by Vatsyayana — social relationships and aesthetics.
Amarakosha was written by Amarasimha — a Sanskrit lexicon.
Panchatantra was written by Vishnu Sharma — animal fables.
Abhijnanasakuntalam was written by Kalidasa — the story of Dushyanta and Shakuntala.
The Abhijnanasakuntalam tells of King Dushyanta and Shakuntala.
Meghaduta was written by Kalidasa — a Yaksha sends a message through a cloud.
In the Meghaduta a Yaksha sends a message to his beloved through a cloud.
Raghuvamsa was written by Kalidasa — the lineage of King Raghu.
Malavikagnimitram was written by Kalidasa — love and court politics (hero: Agnimitra Shunga).
Kumarasambhava was written by Kalidasa — the birth of Kartikeya.
Vikramorvashiyam was written by Kalidasa — Pururavas and Urvashi.
Ritusamhara was written by Kalidasa — a poem on the six seasons.
Kalidasa is traditionally placed among the Navaratnas of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya).
Dashakumaracharita was written by Dandin — adventures of ten princes.
The source dates Dandin's Dashakumaracharita to the 6th–7th century CE; standard references place Dandin at the 7th-century Pallava court.
Charaka Samhita was written by Charaka — medicine (Ayurveda).
Charaka is traditionally placed at the court of Kanishka.
Sushruta Samhita was written by Sushruta — surgery.
The Surya Siddhanta is an astronomy text on planetary motion, eclipses and time.
Brihat Samhita was written by Varahamihira — an encyclopedia of astronomy and astrology.
Pancha Siddhantika was written by Varahamihira — summary of five astronomical systems.
Swapnavasavadattam was written by Bhasa — a drama on King Udayana.
Kiratarjuniya was written by Bharavi.
Shishupalavadha was written by Magha.
Uttararamacharita was written by Bhavabhuti — an 8th-century drama.
Vakyapadiya was written by Bhartrihari — philosophy of language.
Ashtanga Hridaya was written by Vagbhata — Ayurveda.
Harshacharita was written by Banabhatta — a biography of Harsha.
Kadambari was written by Banabhatta — completed by his son Bhushanabhatta.
Banabhatta's son Bhushanabhatta completed the Kadambari.
Nagananda was written by Harshavardhana — a Buddhist drama based on Bodhisattva Jataka tales.
Ratnavali was written by Harshavardhana — a romantic court drama.
Priyadarsika was written by Harshavardhana — love, separation and reunion.
Si-yu-ki (Record of the Western World) was written by Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) — in Chinese.
